title: Realism's Project
description: Showing society, refusing the romantic, the disciplined eye

concepts.title: What Realism Wanted
concepts.contentHtml:
Mid-19th-century realism was a deliberate reaction against Romantic fiction. Where Romantic novels indulged sublime emotion, exotic settings, idealised heroes, supernatural events, Realism committed to ordinary people, recognisable settings, plausible psychology, scrupulous attention to social detail.

The realist programme: depict society as it is. Money, class, work, marriage as economic arrangement, the everyday textures of household and street. Refuse the consoling lies of romance.

Major Realists: Stendhal, Balzac, Flaubert in France; Dickens, George Eliot, Trollope, Thackeray in Britain; Tolstoy and Dostoevsky in Russia (with complications); Howells, James, Wharton in America.

concepts.title: The Disciplined Eye
concepts.contentHtml:
Realist technique requires sustained attention to actual conditions of life. Balzac's painstaking inventories of Parisian apartments, listing every piece of furniture and its provenance. Flaubert's dictum le mot juste — the right word, refused decoration. George Eliot's analyses of provincial English society's microeconomics.

This wasn't just description. It was the claim that ordinary life seriously observed could carry the moral and intellectual weight earlier fiction had located in heroic action.

The technique demanded discipline. The Romantic temptation — toward the exotic, the high-toned, the spiritually intense — was constant. Realism was harder than the Romantic mode it rejected.

concepts.title: Auerbach's Mimesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Erich Auerbach's Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1946) is the canonical study of realism as a long Western tradition.

Across twenty chapters, each centred on a single passage from Homer through Virginia Woolf, Auerbach traces how literature has tried to represent ordinary reality. His central argument: realism reaches new depth in 19th-century French fiction, when ordinary contemporary life becomes the proper subject of serious literary treatment.

The book was written in wartime Istanbul exile, without access to a research library. Its scope and confidence are remarkable.

concepts.title: Realism's Politics
concepts.contentHtml:
Realism's commitment to depicting actual society had political consequences.

By showing how class, money, and circumstance actually shape lives, realist fiction implicitly criticised the social order. Balzac's panoramic La Comédie humaine, Dickens's London, Eliot's provincial England, the Russian realists' aristocratic estates — all expose what their societies preferred not to see.

This was politics through observation rather than argument. Lukács in his Marxist criticism celebrated realism precisely because of this — Balzac's monarchism didn't prevent his fiction from anatomising bourgeois capitalism with devastating accuracy.

The realist novel became an instrument of social knowledge in a period when social science was still nascent.

concepts.title: Realism's Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
By 1900 realism's limits were visible to the writers who would become modernists.

The 'realistic' surface had hardened into convention. Stable narrators, omniscient access, chronological plotting were taken to be how serious fiction worked, not as choices among alternatives.

Modernism's response (Joyce, Woolf, Faulkner) was to argue that the inner life of consciousness was just as 'real' as social surface — and that realist conventions had failed to represent it adequately.

Realism didn't die. The realist novel continues to be written. But after modernism it became one option among many, no longer the default form for serious fiction.

title: Flaubert & French Realism
description: Madame Bovary, le mot juste, Balzac's panorama

concepts.title: Balzac
concepts.contentHtml:
Honoré de Balzac (1799-1850) was the foundational French realist. His La Comédie humaine ('The Human Comedy') is a 91-novel sequence with recurring characters depicting French society from the Restoration through the July Monarchy.

Major individual novels: Père Goriot (1835), Lost Illusions (1837-43), Cousin Bette (1846), Eugénie Grandet (1833).

Balzac's mode: encyclopedic. Detailed description of everything — clothes, food, money, furniture, professions, neighbourhoods. Plus relentless plot momentum and characters of operatic intensity. The combination is uniquely his.

concepts.title: Stendhal
concepts.contentHtml:
Stendhal (Henri-Marie Beyle, 1783-1842) wrote a different mode of realism. Faster, more psychological, more ironic.

Major novels: The Red and the Black (1830), The Charterhouse of Parma (1839).

Stendhal's mode anticipates the modern psychological novel. His protagonist Julien Sorel in The Red and the Black is studied with sustained interior attention — his ambition, his self-deception, his romantic intensities — that won't appear again at this density until Dostoevsky.

Stendhal famously dedicated his work 'To the Happy Few' — readers who would understand it. He was right; he was a small audience writer in his lifetime, hugely influential after.

concepts.title: Flaubert
concepts.contentHtml:
Gustave Flaubert (1821-1880) was French realism's most exacting practitioner. Where Balzac wrote 91 novels, Flaubert produced four — and sweated each sentence.

His method: le mot juste, the right word. Flaubert would labour for days over a single paragraph, reading aloud to test rhythm, revising obsessively. Madame Bovary (1856) took five years.

The novel: Emma Bovary, a provincial doctor's wife, romantically destroyed by her own romantic novels and the inadequacy of her marriage. Adultery, debt, suicide.

The famous trial that followed publication — the French government prosecuted Flaubert for offending public morals — established the novel's reputation. He was acquitted; the book became scandalous and successful.

concepts.title: Free Indirect Discourse
concepts.contentHtml:
Flaubert's free indirect discourse made him one of the most influential novelists in the European tradition. The technique — the narrator's voice inflected by a character's without quotation marks — runs continuously through Madame Bovary.

Emma's romantic delusions are filtered through her own grandiose vocabulary, the narrator's distance audible without ever being stated. We see what Emma sees while seeing how Emma is wrong. The double vision is impossible in pure dialogue or pure summary.

French structuralists made Flaubert central to their analysis. Joyce, Woolf, and the modernists worked in his technique whether they acknowledged the debt or not.

concepts.title: Other French Realists
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond the canonical three:

Émile Zola (covered separately under Naturalism).

Maupassant: short-story master, 300+ tales of bourgeois and peasant life. Tight, ironic, often bleak.

The Goncourt brothers: their joint work brought naturalist methods to lower-class subject matter. The Goncourt Prize, awarded annually since 1903, remains French fiction's most important.

Alphonse Daudet, Jules Renard: minor masters of the realist mode.

French 19th-century realism produced more major novelists per square mile of literary culture than any other tradition. The cumulative effect on European fiction was foundational.

title: Russian Realism
description: Tolstoy and Dostoevsky's vast moral worlds

concepts.title: Russian Realism's Distinctness
concepts.contentHtml:
Russian realism in the second half of the 19th century shared technical features with French realism — detailed observation, psychological depth, social panorama — but differed in scope and moral seriousness.

The Russian novel typically engaged philosophical and religious questions French realism handled obliquely. Tolstoy's history-and-individual debate, Dostoevsky's God-and-suffering arguments, Turgenev's nihilism-and-tradition contrasts — all sit closer to ideological content than Flaubertian distance.

The reason is partly political. Russia under the Tsars had no free political speech. Literature took on tasks French and English writers handled in journalism and political tracts.

concepts.title: Tolstoy
concepts.contentHtml:
Lev Tolstoy (1828-1910) is, for many readers, the greatest realist novelist. War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1878) are the central works.

Tolstoy's distinctive technique: total access to characters' minds combined with godlike narrative authority. He moves between hundreds of consciousnesses without losing control. His description has a quality of perfect transparency — the world he constructs feels indistinguishable from the actual one.

Late Tolstoy (after his religious crisis) renounced his earlier work as worldly distraction. The masterpieces remained; his preface to a 1908 edition rejected most of his fiction. The combination of supreme novelist and self-doubting moralist is unique.

concepts.title: Dostoevsky
concepts.contentHtml:
Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821-1881) was Tolstoy's antithesis in mode. Where Tolstoy was serene and panoramic, Dostoevsky was feverish and dialogic.

Major novels: Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot (1869), Demons (1872), The Brothers Karamazov (1880).

His distinctive contribution: polyphony (Bakhtin's term). Multiple voices contend within Dostoevsky's novels without being subordinated to any single authorial perspective. Ivan Karamazov's atheism is voiced so powerfully that critics still debate whether the novel succeeds in answering it.

Dostoevsky also developed a kind of urban realism — Petersburg as feverish, hallucinatory, claustrophobic — that prefigures much modernist technique.

concepts.title: Turgenev and Others
concepts.contentHtml:
Ivan Turgenev (1818-1883) was the third major Russian realist. Less monumental than Tolstoy or Dostoevsky, but technically polished, well-known in Western Europe in his lifetime, friend of Flaubert and Henry James.

His Fathers and Sons (1862) is the canonical novel of generational conflict. Bazarov, the nihilist medical student, became a recognisable type — the Russian intelligentsia's self-image and self-critique.

Goncharov's Oblomov (1859) introduced the figure of the indolent aristocrat — 'oblomovism' becoming a word for a recognisable Russian condition.

Saltykov-Shchedrin's satirical fiction; Leskov's tales; the broader 19th-century Russian realist scene was richer than the canonical 'Tolstoy and Dostoevsky' list suggests.

concepts.title: Why Russia
concepts.contentHtml:
Why did Russia produce so much great realist fiction in such a short period?

Several factors. The serfdom-and-emancipation crisis (serfs freed in 1861) gave novelists urgent social material. The autocracy's restriction on political expression channelled intellectual energy into literature. The Russian Orthodox tradition's seriousness about ultimate questions translated into a fiction unusually attentive to them.

The combination produced what many readers consider the high point of the European novel: a generation of writers who could combine French technical realism with Russian moral seriousness, producing work neither tradition alone would have produced.

Subsequent Russian fiction — through Chekhov, the Soviet century, the post-Soviet present — continues to draw on this legacy. The realist tradition Tolstoy and Dostoevsky established remains active.

concepts.title: American Realism's Late Arrival
concepts.contentHtml:
American realism arrived late compared to European. Through the mid-19th century, American fiction was dominated by romance — Hawthorne's Puritan past, Cooper's frontier, Poe's gothic, Melville's metaphysical voyages.

The realist mode took root after the Civil War, in the post-1865 search for a national literature adequate to a transformed country. The realists' programme: write about the actual America as it was — small towns, growing cities, industrial workers, immigrant populations, the ordinary stuff of life.

concepts.title: William Dean Howells
concepts.contentHtml:
William Dean Howells (1837-1920) was the institutional centre of American realism. Editor of The Atlantic, then Harper's; novelist; friend and champion of both Mark Twain and Henry James.

Major novels: The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885), A Hazard of New Fortunes (1890).

Howells's mode: tactful, careful, mid-toned. His novels handle business ethics, urban housing, marriage, journalism with sustained attention but without the philosophical reach of Tolstoy or the formal extremity of Flaubert. He's been less read in recent decades but was central to his moment.

concepts.title: Henry James
concepts.contentHtml:
Henry James (1843-1916) was the most technically ambitious American realist. Born in New York, lived most of his adult life in England.

Major works: The Portrait of a Lady (1881), The Bostonians (1886), The Ambassadors (1903), The Wings of the Dove (1902), The Golden Bowl (1904).

James's distinctive technique: restricted point of view, sustained psychological depth, prose of extreme nuance. His late novels are notoriously difficult — labyrinthine sentences, deferred meanings, climactic moments rendered through the thinnest perceptual differences.

The 'international theme' — innocent Americans encountering complicated Europeans — runs through much of his work. James lived the contrast he dramatised.

concepts.title: Mark Twain
concepts.contentHtml:
Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens, 1835-1910) developed a different kind of realism — the realism of vernacular speech.

The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1885) is the founding novel of American vernacular literary prose. Hemingway's claim — 'all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn' — overstates the case but captures something real.

The novel's racial politics are more complicated than its early defenders allowed. The N-word appears constantly; Jim's characterisation has been criticised as well as defended; the ending's reversion to Tom Sawyer's pranks reduces Jim to a pawn. The book's status as central American novel and as racially troubling text are both true.

concepts.title: Edith Wharton
concepts.contentHtml:
Edith Wharton (1862-1937) was the major realist novelist of upper-class American society around 1900.

Major novels: The House of Mirth (1905), Ethan Frome (1911), The Age of Innocence (1920, Pulitzer 1921 — first to a woman).

Wharton's territory: Old New York's upper class, its codes, its cruelties to those who failed to navigate them. Lily Bart in The House of Mirth destroys herself by trying to maintain dignity in a system that requires sacrifice of dignity. The Countess Olenska in Age of Innocence doesn't quite escape but gives the novel's central male protagonist an alternative he doesn't take.

Wharton's reputation has risen continuously since the 1970s feminist recovery. She is now read alongside James and Twain as central to American realism.

title: Naturalism
description: Zola, Crane, Dreiser — heredity, environment, the experimental novel

concepts.title: Naturalism's Programme
concepts.contentHtml:
Naturalism emerged from realism in the late 19th century with a more explicit theoretical programme.

The basic claim: human behaviour is the product of heredity, environment, and historical circumstance. Free will, romantic love, individual moral struggle are at most epiphenomena of underlying material forces. The novelist's job is to depict these forces with scientific accuracy.

Sources: Darwin (heredity), Marx (economic determinism), the broader scientific naturalism of the late 19th century. Naturalism was realism with a more aggressive philosophical undercarriage.

concepts.title: Zola
concepts.contentHtml:
Émile Zola (1840-1902) was naturalism's central figure. His twenty-volume Rougon-Macquart sequence (1871-1893) traced two branches of a single family across the French Second Empire.

Major individual novels: L'Assommoir (1877, on Parisian working-class alcoholism), Germinal (1885, on coal-miner strikes), Nana (1880, a courtesan's career), La Bête humaine (1890, on hereditary criminality).

Zola's method: extensive research. He visited mines, factories, brothels, taking notes on conditions. The novels combine documentary detail with melodramatic plot.

Zola also wrote 'J'Accuse...!' (1898), the open letter that broke open the Dreyfus Affair. He was prosecuted, fled to England, returned. The letter is one of the most consequential pieces of journalism ever published.

concepts.title: American Naturalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Naturalism crossed the Atlantic in the 1890s and 1900s.

Stephen Crane (1871-1900): Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893), The Red Badge of Courage (1895). Wrote naturalist fiction, sometimes verging on impressionism. Died at 28.

Frank Norris (1870-1902): McTeague (1899), The Octopus (1901). Heredity-and-economic-determinism in California settings.

Theodore Dreiser (1871-1945): Sister Carrie (1900), An American Tragedy (1925). Long, slow, plain-style novels about ambitious working-class characters destroyed by social and economic forces.

American naturalism tended toward the bleak. The genre's view of human agency was unflattering; its plots usually ended in failure or worse.

concepts.title: Naturalism's Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
Naturalism's theoretical commitments — that fiction should depict deterministic forces with scientific accuracy — had aesthetic costs.

The novels can feel programmatic. Characters become illustrations of theses; plot becomes the machinery of decline. Zola's best work transcends this; much naturalist fiction doesn't.

The 20th century mostly moved past explicit naturalism. The deterministic frame survived in modified forms — sociological fiction, social realism, certain strains of crime and noir fiction. But the rigid Zola-Dreiser programme aged less well than the looser realism it grew out of.

concepts.title: Realism Now
concepts.contentHtml:
Realism survived modernism. Most contemporary literary fiction is broadly realist — characters who seem like real people, plots that work through plausible psychology, settings that feel like actual places.

What has changed: the realist mode is one option among many. Writers can choose realism with awareness of its conventions; or hybridise it with magical realism, autofiction, speculative elements, metafictional play.

Major contemporary realists: Jonathan Franzen, Marilynne Robinson, Elizabeth Strout, Tessa Hadley, Hilary Mantel (in her historical mode), Elena Ferrante. The list could be longer.

Realism as the default for serious fiction is over. Realism as a continuing tradition is robust.
